nameStory: Microthamnion gets its name from Greek words meaning 'small shrub,' describing how this tiny algae forms branching, shrub-like colonies under the microscope. The species name honors Friedrich Traugott Kützing, a 19th-century German botanist who was one of the first scientists to seriously study and classify algae. Though you'd never guess from its grand scientific name, this is actually one of nature's most humble organisms!
description: Microthamnion is a microscopic green algae that forms thin, hair-like filaments you might notice as a greenish film or coating on damp surfaces. **[Uncertain claim: This description is based on general knowledge of microalgae, as specific reference material is unavailable]** Individual plants are invisibly small, but colonies can create patches several inches across that feel slightly slippery to the touch. You'll need a hand lens or microscope to see the beautiful branching structure that gives this algae its 'little shrub' name. It's one of those easily-overlooked organisms that's probably much more common than its low observation count suggests.

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Forms thin, greenish films or coatings on damp rocks, soil, or tree bark that feel slightly slimy when touched

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright to yellowish-green when fresh and moist, becoming darker or brownish when dried out

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Slippery or slightly mucilaginous feel when wet, becoming crusty or flaky when dry

idTips.label: Location preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on surfaces that stay consistently damp but not waterlogged

idTips.label: Microscopic structure
idTips.description: Under magnification, shows branching thread-like filaments resembling tiny green shrubs

habitat: **[Uncertain claim: Habitat details based on general microalgae ecology]** Look for this tiny algae on consistently moist surfaces like shaded rock faces, the north sides of trees, or damp soil in forested areas throughout New England. It prefers spots that get indirect light and stay humid - think of those perpetually damp rocks near streams or the base of trees in dense woods. You're most likely to find it in areas with good air circulation but protection from direct sun and drying winds.

seasonality.spring: Most visible as warming temperatures and spring rains create ideal growing conditions, appearing as fresh green films on damp surfaces.
seasonality.summer: May become less obvious during dry spells but persists in consistently moist, shaded locations. Look for it after rain showers when it appears most vibrant.
seasonality.fall: Often quite active during the humid fall season, taking advantage of increased moisture from autumn rains and reduced evaporation.
seasonality.winter: Survives harsh weather by going dormant, but may remain faintly visible as dried, crusty patches that will green up again with moisture.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye as individual organisms, colonies of Microthamnion can actually help prevent soil erosion by creating a living 'glue' that binds soil particles together - making this microscopic algae a tiny but mighty environmental engineer!
confusionNotes: **[Uncertain claim: Confusion species based on general knowledge]** Often confused with other green algae films or even young moss growth on damp surfaces. The key difference is that Microthamnion feels distinctly slippery when wet, while mosses have a more textured, fuzzy feel even when small. If it looks like a green stain that's slippery to touch, think algae; if it has any visible structure or feels rough, think moss.
contextualKnowledge: **[Uncertain claim: Based on general algae knowledge]** Many people don't realize that what they dismiss as 'green slime' or 'algae scum' on rocks and trees actually represents dozens of different species, each with their own specific habitat needs and ecological roles. Microthamnion is part of this hidden world of microorganisms that most nature guides skip over entirely.
compareHints: **[Uncertain claim: No related species data available]** Since no other Microthamnion species are recorded in our New England dataset, compare this with other filamentous green algae by looking for the characteristic slippery texture and preference for consistently moist (not soaking wet) surfaces. Unlike pond or stream algae, terrestrial species like this one rarely form the long, stringy masses you'd see in water.
